What is the displacement during the last 2 seconds of the motion?
A
6 m
B
12 m
C
18 m
D
24 m

hints: Look at the time axis and isolate the last 2 seconds: this is the interval from $t = 2 \text{ s}$ to $t = 4 \text{ s}$, where the graph rises from $6 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ to $12 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
Recall that for a velocity-time graph the displacement equals the area under the graph, so focus on the area of the strip between $2 \text{ s}$ and $4 \text{ s}$.

Treat that strip as a trapezium with parallel sides $6 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $12 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and width $2 \text{ s}$, or as a rectangle plus a triangle, then calculate $\frac{1}{2} \times \text{sum of parallel velocities} \times \text{time}$.
walkthrough: Identify the required interval. The motion lasts $4 \text{ s}$, so the last $2 \text{ s}$ is from $t = 2 \text{ s}$ to $t = 4 \text{ s}$.
Read the velocities from the straight-line graph. At $t = 2 \text{ s}$, $v = 6 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and at $t = 4 \text{ s}$, $v = 12 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
State the rule: displacement equals the area under a velocity-time graph, so displacement $= $ area between $t = 2 \text{ s}$ and $t = 4 \text{ s}$.
Set up the area as a trapezium: $\text{area} = \frac{1}{2} \times (6 + 12) \times (4-2)$ with velocity in $\text{m s}^{-1}$ and time in $\text{s}$.
Calculate: $\frac{1}{2} \times 18 \times 2 = 18$, and units of $\text{m s}^{-1} \times \text{s}$ give $\text{m}$, so displacement $= 18 \text{ m}$.

A.explanation: 6 m is too small and corresponds to only part of the area, such as the small triangle above $6 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ rather than the total area from $t = 2 \text{ s}$ to $t = 4 \text{ s}$.

B.explanation: 12 m would be the area of a $6 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ by $2 \text{ s}$ rectangle, which ignores that velocity rises from $6 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ to $12 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ during this interval.

C.explanation: The area under the graph from $t = 2 \text{ s}$ to $t = 4 \text{ s}$ is $\frac{6+12}{2} \times 2 = 18 \text{ m}$, which equals the displacement.

D.explanation: 24 m is $12 \text{ m s}^{-1} \times 2 \text{ s}$, which treats the velocity as constant at its maximum value instead of finding the trapezium area.
